full_story_part1_c1.canonical_text: You call me mad? I am perfectly sane. My illness sharpened my senses; it did not weaken my mind. I hear everything in heaven and earth. Listen, and judge how calmly I tell you what happened. The old man shared my house. I loved him; he had never hurt me, and I wanted none of his money. Only his eye troubled me: pale blue, with a cloudy film. A vulture's eye. You understand? That eye had to go. For seven nights, at midnight, I opened his bedroom door so slowly that it made no sound. Then I let a thin ray from my lantern touch his face. Always, the eye was closed. What could I do? I hated the eye, not the man. On the eighth night, I smiled at my own patience. Then my thumb slipped against the lantern fastening.

full_story_part2_c3.canonical_text: I stood still for an hour. Imagine such control! He remained awake, listening. Once, he gave a small groan of terror. I knew that sound from my own sleepless nights. At last, I opened the lantern a little. The ray fell upon the eye. Wide open. Then I heard his heart—a low, quick beat, like a watch wrapped in cotton. It grew faster. Louder. Surely a neighbour would hear! I rushed in. He shrieked once before I dragged him down and pulled the heavy bed over him. Soon the beating stopped. I checked. He was dead. I hid his body beneath three floorboards and replaced them perfectly. No stain, no mark. Would a madman have worked so neatly?

full_story_part3_c1.canonical_text: At four, three police officers knocked. A neighbour had heard a shriek. I welcomed them. The cry was mine, I explained: a bad dream. The old man was away in the country. I showed them every room, then brought chairs into his bedroom. My own chair stood directly above the body. You see how little I feared? They sat chatting. Soon my ears began to ring. Beneath their voices came a low, quick beating. I talked louder. I stood and paced, scraping my chair across the boards. Still it grew louder. Louder! The officers went on smiling and talking. Not one seemed to hear. Yet they must hear! They knew. Their easy smiles were mocking me. How could you expect me to sit there and bear it? "I did it!" I screamed. "Tear up the planks! Here, beneath my chair! It is the beating of his hideous heart!"
